name: Aluette
description: Aluette is a four-player French trick-taking game using a 48-card Spanish-suited pack with a fixed rank order where suits are irrelevant for trick strength.

overview.description: Aluette is a four-player French trick-taking game using a 48-card Spanish-suited pack with a fixed rank order where suits are irrelevant for trick strength.

history.origins: Aluette is associated with Vendee and the Brittany coast, with possible roots in late medieval Luettes or a later Spanish-merchant influence via Nantes.
timeline: Late 15th c.: Luettes in SW France
17th c.: Possible Spanish-merchant introduction in Nantes
Modern English rules documented by John McLeod with historical analysis by Thierry Depaulis
history.cultural: La Vache (the cow); 3s, 2s, aces high as in Truc/Put; partner signalling.

setup.players: Four in two fixed partnerships, partners opposite. Deal and play clockwise.
setup.deck: 48-card Spanish pack (A, K, Cavalier, Jack, 9, 8, 7, 6, 5, 4, 3, 2 in each suit) with Aluette fixed rank order.
setup.dealing: First dealer by deal-until-high-four (monsieur/madame vs borgne/vache); madame deals first. Nine cards each in batches of three; 12 left (optional chanter: 6 each to left of dealer and dealer, then each discards 6).
setup.equipment: 48-card Spanish-suited pack (Aluette designs); optional score sheet.

rules.objective: Your team wins the point if one of you takes more tricks than any other single player; if tied, the first to have reached that trick count wins the point for the team.
rules.gameplay: Left of dealer leads; no suit obligation. Highest card wins trick (ties = trick spoiled, same player leads again). Nine tricks. First to 3 tricks turns a card face up; first to 3 turns two up (to remember order for ties). Partners may signal by agreed gestures.
keyRules: 48 cards; fixed ranking; no trumps; tricks not pooled by partnership
Ties for high = spoiled trick; first to most tricks wins point for team
Signals allowed; chanter optional (extra 6 cards each to two players, discard to 9)

strategy.basic: Last to play has advantage (voir venir); first two often play low, third may play high, fourth beats or spoils. Spoil to keep lead with partner.
strategy.intermediate: Signal only when partner needs the information; avoid signalling when your hand is strong (helps opponents). Support partner's mordienne by spoiling and spreading tricks.
strategy.advanced: Surrender offer and mordienne commitment; announced mordienne (variant) extends match to 10 points.
tips: Learn the core trick-taking and fixed-rank tactics without using signals first, then layer in the traditional gesture system described in French rulebooks such as those by Rebour.

variations.name: Chanter
variations.description: If all agree, dealer and player to dealer's left each receive six extra cards and discard six back to nine-card hands.
variations.emptyOverridesReason: This variation only affects who receives extra cards and which cards are discarded before play; the core engine loop and scoring rules remain unchanged.

variations.name: Announced Mordienne
variations.description: Mordienne must be announced in advance and match may be played to 10 points.
variations.emptyOverridesReason: Announced mordienne changes match length and bonus scoring, which are documented in rules and scoring text but not yet parameterized as separate engine overrides.

scoring.description: Team of the individual with most tricks (or first to that count) gets 1 point. Match = 5 deals; higher total wins. Mordienne: win with a run of consecutive tricks at the end after none earlier = 2 points. Surrender possible; refusal commits opponents to mordienne or give 2 to surrendering team.
scoring.winCondition: Your team wins the point if one of you takes more tricks than any other single player; if tied, the first to have reached that trick count wins the point for the team.
